[Traffic Advisory] NOTICE OF ROUTINE MAINTENANCE ON M1 AND M2 MOTORWAYS

@MyJRA wishes to inform road users of the routine maintenance currently underway on the M1 (northbound and southbound) between Grayston Drive and Shakespeare Avenue Bridge, and on the M2 (eastbound and westbound) from Lower Germiston Road to Main Reef Road. Roadwork will be active until the 30th of October 2025.  

Lane closures will be effected from 09h30 - 15:00 during weekdays and between 07h30 – 16h00 on weekends. 

Traffic delays are expected along the M1 and M2 sections during the maintenance period, therefore motorists are advised to plan their journey in advance, exercise caution on the roads and reduce their travelling speed for the safety of our maintenance teams and other road users.  We thank all road users in advance for their patience and cooperation. 
#JoburgRoads #JoburgUpdates ^NJ

data.text:
Dewey's Beatdown
MANILA BAY
May 1 1898

The Spanish-American War became a two Ocean naval war. For once in her history, America was prepared. Her Navy was three times as large as Spain's and was far more efficient. The American Navy had four first class Battleships against Spain's one, which was in drydock. Her cruisers and other warships were vastly better equipped and served than those of the Spanish Navy.

Never before or since has the American Navy sailed into battle with such superiority and much of this was due to the theories of Captain Mahan and the driving energy of Theodore Roosevelt, Assistant Secretary of the Navy.

Rear Admiral Patrico Pasaron, commander of the Spanish squadron in Manila Bay was like most Spanish officers; utterly brave and utterly defeatist. To prevent the bombardment of Manila, he stationed his seven ships in shallow water. There, in gloomy resolution, he awaited the powerful Americans.

American Commadore George Dewey quickly cleared his decks for battle.  The seven Spanish ships were in line. The Spanish fired first, wild and high. At that Commadore Dewey said, "You may fire when ready..." At a distance of 5,500 yards, Olympia's 8-incher belched smoke and flame. Soon all American ships were firing, deliberately and with slow majesty. Dewey paraded his bellowing ships before the Spanish ships. Five times they promenaded, three times west and twice east, until the smoke of battle obscured the stricken enemy.

Dewey broke off action for breakfast. At 11:16am, Dewey stood ready to renew the battle. By then the Spanish was dying, it was a blazing shambles. 
It was all over. Dewey's squadron took up unchallenged command of the bay, masters of Manilla and of the entire Philippine Archipelago as well. 

In seven hours, with not a man killed and only eight slightly wounded, the United States of America had become a world power.
